title: EU AI Act transparency rules go live — Commission's enforcement toolkit activates
subtitle: August 2 marked the switch from countdown to enforcement — Article 50 chatbot and deepfake disclosures are now legally binding, and the AI Office can now demand information, model access, and product recalls.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The European Commission confirmed that Article 50 of the AI Act became enforceable on August 2, alongside the general-purpose AI (GPAI) rules and the governance chapter that empowers the AI Office. From that date, any AI system that talks to people in the EU must tell them they are talking to a machine unless it is obvious from context, and deepfakes and manipulated audio, image or video must be disclosed as artificially generated. The rules apply to providers and deployers, whether the underlying model is proprietary or open-weight, and whether the company is based inside the bloc or not.

The enforcement machinery is what actually changed on August 2. The AI Office, together with national market surveillance authorities, can now issue formal information requests, demand access to models for testing, order recalls, and levy administrative fines. For GPAI providers, the ceiling is up to 3% of worldwide annual turnover or €15 million, whichever is higher. The Commission spent the past year publishing a Code of Practice, a template chatbot disclosure format, and Q&A guidance to give companies runway — that runway has ended, and the formal request-and-response cycle can start immediately.

One thing did not turn on. Under the Digital Omnibus deal finalized on June 29, most Annex III high-risk obligations — the classification, documentation, conformity assessment, and human oversight requirements for standalone systems used in recruitment, credit scoring, education, law enforcement, border control and critical infrastructure — slid to December 2, 2027, a seventeen-month extension. AI embedded in regulated products under Annex I moves to August 2, 2028. Article 50(2)'s machine-readable marking of synthetic outputs also has a four-month grace for systems already on the market before August 2, applying fully from December 2. The result is a two-speed AI Act: transparency now, high-risk in fifteen to twenty-four months.

For learners: the disclosure obligations that landed this weekend are cheap to comply with and expensive to ignore. A chatbot needs a first-interaction notice ('you're chatting with an AI'). AI-generated media needs a visible label. If you ship anything users touch in Europe, walk through your product today, count the surfaces that fall under Article 50, and add the notices. The high-risk regime is a much bigger project, but you now have more than a year to plan for it — a rare gift in AI policy, and one worth using rather than assuming it will slip again.
